newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bankruptcies soar as economic recovery slow.
newsitem.headline: Japan bankruptcies soar as economic recovery slow.

text.p: Corporate Japan has suffered a steep rise in business failures as the nation"s giant economy struggles to achieve a solid recovery.
Private credit research agency Tokyo Shoko Research Ltd reported on Friday that the number of bankruptcies in the month rose nearly 10 percent compared with last year to 1,236.
It was the 48th month in a row the number has exceeded 1,000.
Total debts held by businesses that went bust in January more than doubled, as firms sank under the weight of debts left over from the free-wheeling 1980s "bubble" economy era, Tokyo Shoko said.
Bankruptcies increased in all industry sectors except for the retail and service sectors and a total of 14,524 Japanese workers lost their jobs because of the failures.

"The trend is that, in addition to companies which suffered from the bubble and small firms unable to cope with industrial structural reforms, middle-tier companies, which are exhausted by prolonged economic sluggishness, have also started to become insolvent," Tokyo Shoko said.
The January bankruptcies included that of Kyotaru Co Ltd, a sushi restaurant chain in mid January with estimated debts of 101.3 billion yen ($810 million).
Kyotaru was the first company listed on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange to fail since mid-1993.

The failure was taken as a sign that Japan Inc was still in trouble, and analysts see the scale of Japanese bankruptcies remaining high and the outlook bleak as the country"s huge economy struggles to achieve a solid recovery.
Also in January, Coco Yamaoka Hoshokuten, which specialised in diamond jewellery, was declared bankrupt, with debts of 60 billion yen ($480 million).
Non-bank financial firms Sanwa Tatemono Sogo Finance Co Ltd and CS Sogo Service Kabushiki Kaisha also failed.

All four firms suffered as a result of aggressive business practices during the bubble era but the number of companies affected by the prolonged economic slump that followed the bubble was increasing as well, Tokyo Shoko said.
About 60 percent of bankruptcies in January resulted from factors which Tokyo Shoko said were typical in a slow economy: sluggish sales, accumulated losses and unpaid bills. ($1=125 yen)
